newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Germany pledges support for Romania NATO, EU entry.
newsitem.headline: Germany pledges support for Romania NATO, EU entry.

text.p: Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Wednesday said Germany was ready to throw its weight behind Romania's longshot drive to win early admission to NATO and the European Union.
"Germany will support you as much as it can along the path to Euro-Atlantic institutions," Kinkel told a joint session of parliament's two chambers at the start of a two-day visit.
"Germany remains an advocate for Central and East European countries, Romania included, in their attempts to move closer to Euro-Atlantic organisations."
Kinkel's remarks appeared to end Bonn's coolness over supporting Romania's rapid integration into the western alliance.
Most countries on NATO's southern flank, including France and Italy, back Romania's bid to be included in the first expansion wave to be announced at a July summit in Madrid.

The United States, Britain and Germany have been more restrained, declining to support Bucharest openly. A U.S. State Department official said last week that Washington would not decide until May or June which countries to back.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites for inclusion. Romania's chances have improved since reformists ousted ex-communists in elections last November, and Slovenia is also regarded as a longshot hope.
Russia, opposed to expansion, hopes to sign a treaty next month setting down the terms of a special relationship with the Alliance and rejects any military buildup in new member-states.

Kinkel, greeted by huge applause, said Romania's campaign for early membership "is on the table at the summit and will be examined very carefully. Romania's big progress over the past few years will play an important role."
He later told reporters after meeting Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea there was "no doubt Romania will become a member of the EU and NATO and I would like this to happen as soon as possible".
But he said any forecast on which countries might be asked to join in July would be "mere speculation".

In his speech to parliament, Kinkel praised the government's public commitment to market reforms after seven years of what Romanian and Western experts regard as foot-dragging under the previous leftist administration.

He said Romania had played a "stabilising role" in central Europe with the conclusion of a treaty last year with longstanding rival Hungary. A similar accord is planned with the former Soviet republic of Ukraine.

Kinkel's visit to Romania marks five years since the two states signed a post-communist treaty. It also marks 30 years since Romania formally recognised the old West Germany after World War Two, the first communist country to do so.

Romania was the first former Warsaw Pact state to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme. It has an association agreement with the EU but President Emil Constantinescu acknowledges that EU membership remains a long-term goal.
